text: Lesson 9 established that Source Control Integration connects a scoped application's files to an external Git repository. The actual connection happens at the application record level in Studio: the scoped application gets linked to a specific repository URL, hosted on a provider like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. That repository becomes the application's source of truth for its code going forward, alongside, not instead of, the application record living inside the instance.

This is conceptually the same thing a developer does on any other software project when they clone or initialize a repository for a new codebase. The difference here is that the codebase is a ServiceNow scoped application, and the project folder is the application's component records — scripts, business rules, UI pages, and the rest — as Studio manages them.

A Git repository doesn't accept pushes from just anyone. Connecting an application to a repository means configuring real credentials so ServiceNow can authenticate as a user, or service account, with push and pull access. That credential effectively has write access to the application's entire codebase, so it deserves the same care any other production credential gets.

Once the connection is authenticated, two directions of movement become possible. Push sends changes made inside the instance out to the repository as a real commit. Pull brings changes that exist in the repository, like a merged pull request, back into the instance, updating the application's records to match. That's the same push and pull vocabulary any developer already uses on any other Git-based project.

Before this connection exists, an application's code can only move between instances by hand, through Update Sets, or inside Studio. After it exists, that application behaves like any other software project: committed, pushed, branched, and pulled using habits a development team already has. Not a new skill from scratch — the same Git workflow this catalog has already taught, now pointed at a ServiceNow application. Next: a worked lab walking through exactly that workflow.
